s17.slug: FRIDAY · 7:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN THE NAVIGATOR — THE STATIONS
body: St. Brendan’s keeps its lights low for the Stations: the sanctuary lamp, the two banks over the side aisles, and the rest of the church given back to the evening going violet in the high windows. The purple is everywhere else. It’s on the cloth at Mary’s feet where the flowers used to be, on the ambo, on the stole around Father Osei’s neck as he comes out of the sacristy behind the cross. Maybe forty people. On a Sunday night the place takes four hundred standing, and the forty have spread themselves through it with the Catholic instinct for the back half.

Joey Abruzzo has the cross. It’s the brass processional cross on its pole, a head taller than he is, and he carries it in both fists with his elbows out, and when he grounds it at the first station the knock goes up into the rafters and comes back down, and a woman in the middle pews jumps. He is too loud even holding a cross. Two acolytes from the nine o’clock come behind him with candles, the flames laid back by the walking.

The stations go round the walls, seven to a side, dark carved wood, the figures rubbed pale at the knees and knuckles by people touching them on the way past for longer than anybody here has been alive. At each one Father Osei names it and says, “We adore you, O Christ, and we praise you,” and the church answers, “Because by your holy cross you have redeemed the world,” and Mrs. Fitch, three pews from the front in her good camel coat, is always a half-step ahead of everybody else, so the answer arrives twice, hers and then theirs, an echo that got there first.

Between the stations, while the little procession turns from one wall toward the next, Gus Ferreira at the organ gives a note with only the soft stops out, and he and five or six voices up front sing a verse of the Stabat Mater in the old English, *At the cross her station keeping*, Gus’s foghorn underneath holding the rest of them up.

Jack came by himself. He walked up the hill from Delgado at a quarter to seven, and he stands at the back by the holy water, near enough the door to feel the cold come in under it. Lena is up front on the aisle in the second pew, the one Kevin said he’d save, with Kevin beside her in his windbreaker. At every station, when Father Osei says the words, she genuflects all the way to the floor, right knee down hard on the tile, and comes back up without a hand on the pew. He sees every one from the back of the church. He tells himself he’s watching the cross.

Day three of the habit told no and the first day of bread and water, and he has had a roll and a half since he woke. Around four o’clock the hunger stopped being in his stomach. Now it’s in his head, a high, thin, ringing clearness, the floor a little farther down than it ought to be and the candle flames a little too sharp at the edges. His hands are the worst of it. They want the breast pocket, where the pack lies flat — he can feel its corner through his shirt when he breathes in — and he keeps them out of it, fists in the side pockets of the Carhartt with the lining balled up inside them.

The third station, the first fall. The fourth, his mother. The fifth, Simon of Cyrene, pulled out of the crowd and made to carry it. At each one the church turns from one wall to the next with a noise of shoes and kneelers, and the cross goes ahead.

At the sixth they come to the wall nearest the door, and Joey grounds the cross not six feet from him. *Veronica wipes the face of Jesus.* In the carving she holds the cloth up in both hands, and the face is on it, small and cut deep, the only face on that wall looking straight out. Father Osei reads the meditation from the booklet and Jack doesn’t hear a word of it. On Wednesday morning in New Orleans the old priest who poured the water on Lena at her baptism pressed ashes onto Jack’s forehead with his thumb, and they went on crooked, and on Thursday morning the last of them went down a steel sink at a truck stop in Fort Stockton. *Wash your face, so that you may not appear to be fasting.* He did what it said. He looks at the cloth in the woman’s hands.
*I haven’t got a cloth,* he prays, which is as far as it gets. *Take the hands.*

At the twelfth station the church goes down on its knees on the bare floor and stays down. Jack kneels on the stone by the door with his fists still in his pockets. Up front, past all the bowed heads, he can see the back of hers, the dark of her hair against the collar of the jean jacket, and that is all he looks at until Father Osei says the words and everybody gets up.

After the fourteenth there is a last prayer and a last verse, and the lights come up a notch, and people start finding their coats and their car keys. Father Osei hands the cross off to the sacristan and comes down the side aisle still in the stole, a little uneven on the left leg, nodding to people as he goes, and he stops at the back by the holy water in front of Jack and looks at him. He takes his time. He looks at Jack’s face, and the color in it, and his eyes, and the two fists in the pockets of the Carhartt, and comes back to the face.
“You look like a man who has driven two thousand miles on no food.”
“Two thousand and six.”
Osei doesn’t smile, quite. “Saturday I hear confessions,” he says. “Three-thirty. Or whenever you knock.” And he goes back up the aisle to see about the candles.

Outside it’s full dark and the cold is coming up the hill off the Channel. Jack stands on the top step. People come out around him in twos and threes and go down to the street. Lena comes out with Kevin a step behind her sorting his keys, and she goes down past Jack, neither slow nor fast, her hands in the pockets of the jean jacket, toward Kevin’s van at the curb.
“One down,” she says, going by, and doesn’t stop.
He stays where he is, fists in the lining, while the van’s doors open and shut and it pulls out and takes the hill. He’s counting too. He has been since the levee.

s17a.slug: SATURDAY · 1:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 — CAN’T
body: The clock on Theo’s side says 1:40. Jack has been on his back on top of his made bed since half past ten, boots off, the Carhartt still on, his hands folded on his stomach where he can see them by the light from the parking lot.

Across the room Theo is breathing slow and even, and every so often the evenness stops, and starts again a little too carefully. It isn’t sleep. Jack doesn’t say anything to it, and it doesn’t say anything to him.

The RAZR lies shut on the desk. The pack is on the desk too, under the crucifix, where he put it at midnight so his thumbnail would quit working at the tab on the cellophane: red and white, sealed, the lot light lying along it.

He has been doing the arithmetic of Tuesday for three hours. What he says first, and where: on the porch, or inside, or after she’s put the plate down. Eggs with ambition. Which chair she puts him in. Whether he lets her feed him first, and how long he can let it run before the letting is its own kind of lie. He gets to the bottom of it and starts again at the top, and it comes out the same every time, and the number won’t get any smaller.
At ten to two he sits up and puts his boots on.

choices.text: *Take the pack to the east stairwell.*

s18p.slug: SATURDAY · 2:05 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE — HER PORCH
body: He goes down Ocean Road with his hands in his pockets and the cold coming through the denim at the knees. At Las Olas a party is going out like a tide: a front door standing open on a hallway of red cups, three boys on the curb sharing the last of a pizza out of the box, a couch dragged onto the lawn with a girl asleep on it under somebody’s letterman jacket, and up on a second-floor balcony another girl singing the chorus of “TiK ToK” down at the parked cars, the same part over and over, with total sincerity. The jasmine on the fences isn’t out yet. Past it Del Playa goes quiet, the ocean-side houses dark against a sky without a star in it, and under their back decks the surf comes in and pulls out.

Her house is dark. He knew it would be; she’s in Burnaby in a makeup chair with somebody gluing a wound onto her neck. The porch still leans a little to the left, toward the neighbors, and the swing hangs at the far end on its chains, and he doesn’t sit in the swing. He sits on her top step. Over the door the porch light is off. Tuesday she’ll leave it on.

By the door her rain boots stand side by side, yellow, the left one with a script rolled up and pushed down inside it to the brads so the wind won’t have it. On the rail there’s a coffee can of beach glass, mostly green and brown, with one blue piece balanced on the top that she must have found last and liked best, because that’s where she put it. He nearly laughs at the boots. Of course she’d keep a script in a boot. She’d keep it where she has to put her foot in it in the morning and remember she has lines.

If he leans out past the post he can see the turnout down the road, the dark scoop of gravel past the Marine Lab fence where the Saab used to sit with the engine off and the heater on and the two of them in it, talking, till the windows went white.

This is where he’ll tell her. On this porch, under that light, in three days, with her standing about where the boots are. He makes himself look at it: the door, the boards, the place she’ll stand. He hasn’t got the first sentence. He has her face when it gets there, and he can’t look at that, so he looks at the blue glass.
The pack is in his breast pocket the entire time, and sitting on her steps with the ocean going in and out under the house, he doesn’t think about it at all. He notices that, and wishes he hadn’t.
The RAZR goes against it. SKYE (MISFIT), on her meal break.

s18s.slug: SATURDAY · 2:05 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE EAST STAIRWELL — NO. 13
body: The push bar is cold under his hand. The east stairwell hasn’t changed: cinderblock painted a cream gone yellow, the steel rail, the fluorescent tube over the landing humming its one note, and the cold that lives in here all year whatever the rest of Delgado is doing. He sits on the third step down from the fourth floor. In January he smoked one on this step at twenty to four in the morning, and nine days after that he sat on it with one in his fingers and put it back.

Up here, past two, the building has gone as quiet as it gets. Somebody’s music comes up the well from a long way down, a bass line and nothing else, and somewhere a toilet runs and runs. The wired-glass window on the landing is black, with his own reflection in it sitting on a step in a Carhartt, which he doesn’t look at long.
He takes the pack out of the breast pocket and turns it end over end on his knee, Kevin’s trick with his BlackBerry. Red and white. The cellophane takes the tube light and gives it back.

It’s the worst hour of the third day and he can feel all of it: the itch along the insides of his forearms that scratching can’t get to, the hollow of a day of bread and water, the fog behind his eyes from three nights of next to nothing, and under all of that the want, so exact he can feel the filter on his lip and the first pull going down to the bottom of him. His thumbnail finds the tab on the cellophane. He gets the nail under it.

He doesn’t pull it. He doesn’t take the nail out either. He sits there with it under the tab and says the St. Michael prayer under his breath, all of it, as it’s printed on the card in his wallet, *defend us in battle, be our protection against the wickedness and snares of the devil*, and it doesn’t make the want go anywhere. It gives his mouth something to do. He says it again.

Three days from now he’ll be on a porch on Del Playa with a woman who is going to make him eggs. He thinks about her laughing at the pack in Blythe — *the most Method thing I’ve ever heard* — and his thumb aches, and he keeps it where it is.
*Whatever you’re doing, Jack — you can stop.*

The tube hums. Somewhere below, a door on the second floor opens and shuts, and somebody laughs in the hall and is gone. He sits with the nail under the tab until his thumb aches, and takes it out, and puts the pack back in the breast pocket over his heart, and zips it.
The RAZR goes against it. SKYE (MISFIT), on her meal break.

s19.slug: SATURDAY · 6:55 AM → 1:00 PM · THE ANCHOR — THE FISHERMEN

body.text: *Come back the twentieth and earn them.* It’s the twentieth. He comes in the Anchor’s back door at five to seven with Gloria’s tin under his arm and his hair still wet, and the kitchen is the kitchen: the Hobart breathing steam, the radio on the shelf over the line playing something low in Spanish, Rudy at the sink with his sleeves pushed up and his rosary on the shelf above it where it lives. The fishermen shift is still his.
body.else: He gave Hector the Saturdays from a front step in New Orleans, and he comes anyway, at five to seven, in the front door with the customers, with Gloria’s tin under his arm and his hair still wet. Through the pass he can see Hector on the Hobart. Gloria looks at him over the case, and at the tin, and points the grease pencil at a stool. “You gave him your Saturdays. Sit.”

body: Gloria is behind the case with the grease pencil pushed through the knot of her hair, giving the pies their quarter-turn, one and then the next, so the good side faces the door. From seven on the bell over the door goes every couple of minutes, and she doesn’t look up for it. She never has.

body.text: The fishermen shift runs seven to one: men off the boats in the harbor with salt in the seams of their hands, who pay in cash and tip in it and want their eggs before they’ve finished sitting down. Merle has his chowder at eight in the morning, as he does, and swears it’s a breakfast food in Gloucester. Jack takes the pit. Day four, no sleep, the habit told no, and the dish pit is a mercy. The racks come and the racks go, the spray arm bangs, the steam comes up into his face, and his hands have a job. They’re too busy to want anything. Rudy, rinsing beside him, watches the speed of him for a while and says, soft, “Mijo. The plates aren’t going anywhere,” and goes back to his pots.
body.else: So he sits. The fishermen come in off the boats at seven with salt in the seams of their hands, paying in cash, and Merle has his chowder at eight in the morning, as he does, and swears it’s a breakfast food in Gloucester, and Hector runs the Hobart faster than Jack ever ran it. Jack sits at the end of the counter with a coffee and nothing for his hands and the pack in his pocket, until a little after nine, when Gloria sets a bus tub of clean silverware and a brick of paper napkins in front of him and walks off. He rolls silverware till one. It’s a mercy. His hands have a job.

body.text: In the lull at ten he sets the tin on the counter by the register — the pie tin with the boysenberry ghost still in the corner — and takes the lid off. Mémère’s pralines, stacked in their squares of wax paper, the pecans gone glassy at the edges. “Lena’s grandmother made them,” he says. “Her mother says a tin goes back full. She says it’s not manners, it’s law.”
body.else: In the lull at ten he sets the tin on the counter by the register — Gloria’s pecan tin — and takes the lid off. Mémère’s pralines, stacked in their squares of wax paper, the pecans gone glassy at the edges. “Lena’s grandmother made them,” he says. “Her mother says a tin goes back full. She says it’s not manners, it’s law.”

body: Gloria takes one. She eats it standing, with her eyes on the case, and chews, and swallows, and wipes her thumb on her apron.
“Nine,” she says. And to the case, not to him: “Thirty years. I never said nine out loud.”
Around eleven Merle leans in at the pass with his empty bowl and looks at Jack a while through the steam. “You get any beads down there?”
“A few.”
“You look like you got run over by the parade, kid.” He sets the bowl in the window and goes back to his stool.
She puts the lid back on the tin and puts the tin under the counter, down by her purse, where nobody on the line is going to get at it, and goes back to the pies.

body.text: He gets Tony’s card out of his wallet from behind his license and puts it on the counter beside the tin. She reads the back, FOR GLORIA in carpenter’s pencil, and turns it over and reads the front, and turns it back. “Tell him I don’t fly,” she says, and puts it in her apron pocket, and it doesn’t come out again.

body: At one the Hobart shuts down with a long sigh, and Rudy hangs his apron on its nail and takes his rosary down off the shelf and puts it in his shirt pocket, and the last of the fishermen counts out his ones on the counter and goes. When the room is empty she puts a slice of the Dutch apple in front of him at the counter with a fork stuck upright in it. It’s Saturday. Nothing stands between him and a slice of pie but himself.
“Eat.” She looks at his face as she looks at a pie through the case glass, to see if it’s set. “You look like a man with somewhere to be.”

response: “Don’t thank me. Come back.” She goes off down the counter with the pot.
He eats every bite, down to the crust at the point, which he has never in his life eaten.

choices.text: “Thank you for letting me come anyway.”
response: “Don’t thank me. Eat.”
He eats. He eats it to the last flake on the plate, and she takes the plate away with the fork still on it.
“Mémère can come say it.” She puts a second slice down next to the first.
He eats both. It takes him until a quarter to two, and Rudy, going out the back with his jacket on, stops to watch him finish the second one, and nods.
“Then you eat the whole slice.”

She stands there till he does, the grease pencil in her hair and her arms folded, and when he puts the fork down on the clean plate she looks at the plate and then at him. “Seven,” she says, and it isn’t clear which of them she means.

s20.slug: SATURDAY · 3:30 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S — THE LINE
body: The late sun comes in gold through the west windows and lies across the pews in long bars, and the dust turns over slowly in it. The Saturday line in Lent is longer than the Saturday line any other time: students down the side aisle in sweatshirts and flip-flops, two old women with their own kneelers’ worth of patience, a man in a Cal Poly jacket with his hands clasped in front of him, a girl reading an examination of conscience off a folded pamphlet and moving her lips. Out in the vestibule Mrs. Fitch is at the desk counting the week’s envelopes in a whisper.

Over the confessional door the little light is on. Under it the card says KNOCK (GENTLY), and under that (AND PROMPTLY), in Father Osei’s capitals, and nothing else now; there’s a strip of cleaner card at the bottom where the tape was.

Lena is in the line ahead of him, four people between them: the two old women, the Cal Poly jacket, the girl with the pamphlet. She’s in the jean jacket, and he can see the square of the tin in its chest pocket from here. She doesn’t turn around. Day four, and he has had Gloria’s pie and no sleep, and he is steadier than he was yesterday and has no skin at all, and he kneels in the back pew and keeps his eyes on the light.
At twenty to four she turns around. She looks at him down the length of the aisle, one look, straight, and turns back.
The door opens and somebody comes out, and she goes in.

Later she comes out. She goes to the side pew by the Marian shrine and kneels there for her penance with her head down, and then she gets up and leaves by the side door, and the side door is behind the back pew, behind him. He hears her go by. He doesn’t turn.

The old women go in, one and then the other. The Cal Poly jacket goes in. The girl with the pamphlet folds it up small and goes in. When it’s his turn Jack stays on his knees and lets the man who came in behind him go first, and the next, a boy with a skateboard under his arm, and a woman in scrubs, and a couple who go in one after the other while the one waiting holds the other’s coat. He lets every one of them go. The bars of sun move up off the pews and onto the wall.
When the last of them has gone out the front, he’s the only one left in the church. Over the choir loft the clock says 4:14. The light over the door stays on.

s21.slug: SATURDAY · 4:15 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, FATHER OSEI’S OFFICE — TWO CHAIRS
s21.music: Nana Ampadu & the African Brothers Band — “Ebi Te Yie”
body: At a quarter past, the confessional door opens and Father Osei puts his head out and looks down the empty aisle at the one man left in the back pew. He looks a good while, at how Jack is kneeling and the color of him and what his hands are doing, and then he says, “Come.”

Not the box. He takes Jack up the side aisle and through the sacristy and down the hall beyond it to his office, where a record is going on the turntable under the window, low, two guitars chasing each other round and round in a high bright knot, and he lifts the needle as they come in, and the room is quiet. Rubber boots by the door with the mud dried pale on them. Books on the floor in towers. On the desk a box of tissues, which lives there for exactly this. In front of the desk two wooden chairs stand side by side, both turned to the crucifix on the wall.
Father Osei takes the purple stole off the back of his desk chair. “In case,” he says, and kisses it and puts it on, and sits down in one of the two chairs, and looks at the crucifix, not at Jack.
Jack sits in the other one. Up close the office smells of the coffee in the pot on the filing cabinet, gone to tar since noon, and of rubber from the boots. His knee is going. He puts his hand on it.
“When did you sleep?” Osei asks. He is still looking at the crucifix.
“I’m good, Father.”
“You say ‘good’ the way my patients said ‘fine,’” says Father Osei. “Well. We will come back to it.”
“Bless me, Father —”

And there’s nothing after it. *It has been* — he knows the next words, he has said them since he was seven — but nothing that goes after them belongs there yet, and he sits with his mouth open on it, and his hands come up off his knees and go back down.
“Then don’t,” Osei says. “Tell me what happened. We will see what it is after.”

He tells him. It comes out in the wrong order, end first. “We’re both — by the end of the week. Both of us. She’s ending it Sunday. Tomorrow. After Mass, to his face. And I’m telling Skye Tuesday, when she lands. To her face.” He has to stop and go back. “On the levee. In New Orleans, the night before Ash Wednesday. We nearly — and we both stopped. The same second. And then we talked till about three in the morning. Everything since October. All of it. And we said nothing till then. Nothing either one of us would have to explain.” He looks at his hands. “So we haven’t.”

He stops because he has run out of air. He has been talking fast and high and getting nowhere, and his hands are shaking on his knees from no sleep and no cigarettes and the bread and water of yesterday, and his eyes are stinging, and he tells himself that’s the no sleep too. The tissues are right there. He doesn’t take one. Father Osei doesn’t offer.

body.text: “Tuesday,” he says. “To her face. I promised her that. In a darkroom. Before I left.”
body.else: “Tuesday,” he says. “To her face. That’s the least she gets.”

body: Osei looks at the crucifix. His hands are folded on his stomach, the wooden rosary on his belt under them. “And what is it you want me to do with that?”
“Nothing,” Jack says, and it’s true. “I’m not asking you if I can, Father. I know. I knew on the levee.”
“All right.”
The radiator ticks. Jack sits there. He knows. That isn’t it, and he can’t get to what it is, and his right hand has found the hem of the Carhartt and is twisting it.
“It’s Skye,” he says. “I love her.”
“I know,” says Father Osei. “I have heard you say so, in that box.”

body.text: “On the levee I said she was the best thing that happened to me this year, except —” He stops, the same place he stopped on the levee. “And I stopped.”
“I told Lena I’d tell Skye all of it, to her face. And I will. And I love her.”
“On the levee I stopped, and let it be quiet. That was the most honest thing I said all night.”
“Mary Catherine,” he says. He has said it out loud maybe four times in his life. “That’s her name. Her real one.”
body.else: “Skye,” he says again, to the crucifix, as though the name might do some of it for him.

body: And then the thing under it.

choices.text: “I was going to marry her someday, Father. Not soon. Someday. I had the chair picked out at my grandmother’s table.”
choices.key: In Father Osei’s office you told him you’d planned to marry Skye someday — you had the chair picked out at your grandmother’s table.
response: “I was going to marry her someday, Father. Not soon. Someday. I had the chair picked out at my grandmother’s table.”

The chair by the radiator at the kitchen table on Glenwood, Nonna’s corner, where she can reach over and fix your collar while you eat. He’d had Skye in it since Christmas. And then Gina’s text, at one in the morning, back in January, and he says it word for word, because he knows it word for word: “*Nonna says Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife.*”

response.text: “I told Skye she said it. She heard it.”

choices.key: In Father Osei’s office you told him what your grandmother said — Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife — and that you’d told Skye, and meant it.

And the rest, because it’s there behind it: not soon. Someday. He’d had a chair for her at the kitchen table on Glenwood, the one by the radiator in Nonna’s corner. He’d had her in it since Christmas.

response: “My grandmother said Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife. I never told Skye. I meant it anyway.”
And the rest, because it’s there behind it: not soon. Someday. A chair at the kitchen table on Glenwood, the one by the radiator in Nonna’s corner.

choices.text: *Say nothing for a while. Let him wait.*
choices.key: In Father Osei’s office you sat a long time without saying anything. Then you told him you’d meant to marry her someday.
response: He doesn’t say anything, and Father Osei lets him not say it. He has sat up with a great many people at this hour of a thing. The clock on the bookshelf goes. Out in the hall somebody sets a stack of hymnals down. Jack’s hand lets go of the hem of the Carhartt.

“I was going to marry her,” he says finally. “Someday. Not soon. I had a chair for her at our kitchen table on Glenwood, by the radiator, in my grandmother’s corner. And my grandmother sent word, at one in the morning, back in January: Maria Caterina is a good name for a wife.” He says it flat, a part number read off an invoice, because that’s the only way it’ll come out.

s21a.slug: SATURDAY · 4:25 PM · FATHER OSEI’S OFFICE — THE SAME DIRECTION
body: Father Osei is quiet a long time. His hand has come to rest on his left knee, the bad one. He takes his reading glasses off by the cord and holds them, and puts them on again.
“And so,” he says.

“And so why.” Jack tries. He opens his mouth to say why, why it’s her and not — why it has to be this, if he loves Skye, and he does — and nothing in him will line up. He has been trying to say it to himself since the levee. He has had two thousand miles.

What he gets to instead is his mother’s kitchen. Over the phone on the wall on Glenwood Avenue there’s a cross-stitch in a dime-store frame, blue thread on cream, a wedding present to his parents from one of Ma’s aunts, and he grew up reading it while he waited for the phone to ring, which in that house was a lot of waiting. He can see the stitches. He says it as it hangs, stitch for stitch:
“*Love does not consist in gazing at each other, but in looking outward together in the same direction.*” He looks at the floor. “Saint-Exupéry. It’s over the phone in my mother’s kitchen.”
Osei waits.

“Skye looks at me,” Jack says. “Father, she looks at me. Nobody ever — she’s the best thing that ever looked at me. She went to Mass to find out what I was doing in there. She knelt. She walked at the March in January, in the cold. She did all that to see me.” His hands are open on his knees and he doesn’t know when that happened. “And Lena looks where I’m looking. That’s all. That’s all it is. She’s looking at the same thing I’m looking at, she always has been, since the first week, and I turn around and she’s there.” He stops. “It doesn’t make Skye less. It makes it worse.”

“Your Frenchman was a pilot,” Osei says, after a while. “He came down in the Sahara once and walked for days with his mechanic before a Bedouin on a camel found them. A man learns which way he is facing in a desert. He does not learn that it is easy.”

body.text: “A man told me Monday not to wait on anybody,” Jack says. “I told him I was done waiting. Now I’m waiting four days.”
Osei very nearly laughs. “Waiting is not the same as waiting *on*.”

body: “In January,” Jack says, “you asked me. To what question.” He hears his own voice in the little room, and it’s slower than it was ten minutes ago, the sentences coming one at a time and in order. “I think the question was which way I’m facing. I don’t know if that’s right. It’s the one I’ve got.”
Osei gives no verdict on it. “Then you have one more question than you had in January,” he says. “That is progress, in my old profession.”

body.text: “On the morning you left,” he says, “I told you the part of you that wished she had not stopped was not sorrow yet — to bring it to me when you could name it.”
“On the morning you left, you told me you were sorry you put it on her,” he says. “You are carrying something else now.”
“You promised me,” he says. “Not till you were back. You are back.”
“The last time you sat with me you could not name what you were carrying,” he says. “Try now.”

body: It isn’t that wish anymore. That one’s gone; he left it on a levee. He looks for what’s there now and finds it, and it’s smaller than he thought, and worse. “That it could’ve been both,” he says. “That I didn’t have to hurt her to tell the truth. That there was some way to do this where she doesn’t find out on her own porch with dinner on the stove.”
“That has a name,” says Father Osei. “It is grief. Grief is not a sin. I cannot absolve it.” He looks at the crucifix. “You carry it — and He carries it with you.”

body.text: And then, gently: “I put water in her hair at a quarter to five in the morning. She shut her eyes. I remember that.”
body.else: And then, gently: “I met her once, at the van, in the dark. I remember that she came.”

body.text: “In January I told you that if you made her the answer you would make her the occasion. I will not say it again. She was never only an occasion. She was a person, and you loved her as one. That is why this costs.”

body: Jack nods at the floor. His eyes are wet, and Osei doesn’t look over.
Father Osei shifts in his chair and looks at his watch, and something comes into his face that Jack has seen across a chessboard.
“Jack,” he says. “You have been in that chair twenty minutes, and you have not confessed one thing.”
He laughs, small, from somewhere low in his belly. And Jack, who would not have bet a dollar there was a laugh in him this week, laughs too, one short helpless sound into the quiet office.

“No,” he says. “No, I — okay.” He sits up. He makes himself do it as Ma taught him, the examination, the small things, honestly, because there aren’t any big ones; he looks and there aren’t. “Ash Wednesday, at one in the morning, Lena’s Nonc Clovis poured me bourbon on the porch, and I drank it so I wouldn’t want a cigarette. The first hour of Lent. I wasn’t drunk. I wanted to be a little.”
Osei nods at the crucifix.
“Thursday morning I snapped at my roommate. For nothing. He was telling me about a coconut.”

body.text: “I said sorry. It was still mine.”
“I didn’t say sorry to him. I said it to a coconut.”
“I never said sorry. I wrote instead.”

body: “I’m fasting Fridays. Bread and water. Partly for God.” He makes himself finish it. “Partly to beat her at it.”

body.text: “I said it out loud in the van so she’d hear it.”
body.else: “I didn’t tell anybody. I still wanted her to find out.”

body: “Fasting out of pride is still fasting,” says Father Osei. “The pride you can leave with me.”

“And the guy she’s seeing. The one she’s ending it with tomorrow.” This one is harder, and he goes slower. “Everybody says he’s a good man, and he is, I think. And somewhere around Arizona I caught myself hoping he’d be a jerk about it. Tomorrow. So I could quit thinking he’s better than me.”
Osei’s hand turns over on his knee, palm up, and lies there. “Is there more?”
There’s one more.

choices.text: “And I bought a pack of cigarettes. I haven’t opened it.”
response: “And I bought a pack of cigarettes,” he says. “In El Paso. I haven’t opened it.”

“That is not a sin,” says Father Osei. “That is a very expensive rosary.” And, mildly: “Keep it in the pocket and keep the hand off it, and if the hand wins one day, come back. A hand is easier to treat than a lung.”

choices.text: “And on the levee I held her inside my coat, before we stopped. I wanted her there.”
response: “And on the levee I held her inside my coat,” he says. “Before we stopped. It was cold. That’s not why. I wanted her there.”

Osei takes that in a moment. “To want is not to consent,” he says. “To be tempted is not to sin. You stopped. If there was a fault, it was standing so long where the wanting had no wall — a small imprudence, and you have told it, and it is told.” He looks at the crucifix. “What you do about Tuesday you have already said is yours. God does not usually waste a trip.”

choices.text: “And I ate two pralines out of a tin that was supposed to go back full, and moved the rest around so it wouldn’t show.”
response: “And I ate two pralines,” he says, “out of a tin that was supposed to go back full. In Arizona. And I moved the rest around so it wouldn’t show.”

This time Osei laughs from the belly and doesn’t stop for a while, his head back, his hand on the bad knee, and Jack sits there red to the ears with the corners of his own mouth gone. “That one,” Osei says, when he can, wiping his eye with the side of his finger, “I will absolve twice.”

s21b.slug: SATURDAY · 4:45 PM · FATHER OSEI’S OFFICE — ƐYƐ
body: “You know you were not required to bring me any of that,” Father Osei says. “The Church asks you for the mortal sins, and you have none. But she is glad when you bring the small ones. A doctor likes to see the healthy patient too — it is how he learns what healthy looks like — and a small cut bleeds a long time when nobody looks at it. It teaches your conscience its own handwriting.” He turns his head and looks at Jack for the first time since they sat down. “And it lets Him heal what you would have called nothing.”

Jack says the Act of Contrition from memory, Ma’s, the one she taught him at the kitchen table on Glenwood with her hand on the oilcloth beside his so he wouldn’t rush it. *O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended Thee.* He doesn’t rush it. *and I detest all my sins because of Thy just punishments, but most of all because they offend Thee, my God, who art all good and deserving of all my love.* He gets to *the near occasion of sin* and stops, because that’s the end of it.
Father Osei raises his right hand over him. No screen, no box; the late light in the office window behind them both and the crucifix in front.

“God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
Something in Jack’s shoulders that has been up around his ears since Fort Stockton comes down. He doesn’t do anything to make it.
“For your penance,” says Father Osei. “On Tuesday, before you go up that hill, say an Our Father for her. Slowly.” He lets his hand down. “For her. Not for you.”

body.text: “I offered Lent for her,” Jack says. “On Wednesday.”
“Then Tuesday’s Our Father is a bead on the same string.”

body: He takes the stole off and kisses it and folds it over his arm, and sits back. “Did you eat today?”
“Gloria made me.”

“Then she has done my job.” He gets up, one hand on the arm of the chair for the knee. “Go and sleep. A man should not tell the truth on four hours’ sleep; it comes out crooked.” At the door he stops with his hand on the frame. “Ɛyɛ,” he says. “It is well.”

He hangs the purple stole on the hook for the vigil — the five o’clock is his — and goes to vest, and on his way past the turntable he sets the needle back down on the record, and the two guitars pick up where they left off, chasing each other round, as Jack goes out. The sacristy hall smells of candle wax and floor polish. Up in the tower the bell starts for the vigil.

s22.slug: SATURDAY · 5:00 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE FRONT STEPS
body: The first Saturday evening of Lent comes down gold over the courtyard, where the sprinkler is still in pieces on a tarp by the fountain with a pipe wrench lying across it. Behind him, through the doors, the organ starts and the people inside stand up and sing the opening hymn, “Lord, Who Throughout These Forty Days,” the hymn coming through the doors thin and steady.

A family comes up the steps past him late, a father carrying a little boy asleep on his shoulder with one shoe off, the mother behind with the shoe, and they go in, and the hymn comes out the door with them for a moment and is shut back in. The sun is down behind the bell tower. The cold that comes up the hill at this hour hasn’t got here yet.

He sits down on the top step. His hands are on his knees, doing nothing, and they don’t want anything to do. He takes the pack out and turns it over and looks at it, the red, the white, the seal, and puts it back in the breast pocket over his heart and zips it.
Tomorrow is Sunday. It isn’t his.
The RAZR goes. SKYE (MISFIT), before her call time.

s22a.slug: SATURDAY · 5:10 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE FRONT STEPS
body: He shuts the phone and puts it back in the breast pocket over his heart, next to the pack.
Inside, the hymn ends, and there’s the sound of a church sitting down. At the bottom of the hill the Channel takes the last of the gold and holds it a minute, and lets it go.
He gets up and goes in at the back as the first reading begins, and stands where he stood last night, by the holy water, with the lit church in front of him.
Three days.
